t.6.34.1: While the monkeys and the Rākṣasas were still fighting, the sun went to its setting, and a night that would take away lives set in.
t.6.34.3: Crying "You are a rākṣasa!", the monkeys, and crying "You are a monkey!", the rākṣasas, struck one another in battle in that dreadful darkness.
t.6.34.2: Then a night battle broke out between the elephants and the Rākṣasas, fierce warriors bound in enmity toward one another, each eager for victory.
t.6.34.4: "Kill! Tear apart! Come here!" and "Why do you run away?" Such a most tumultuous uproar was heard in that darkness.
t.6.34.5: In that darkness the black Rākṣasas, clad in golden armour, appeared like lordly mountains whose forests of herbs are ablaze with light.
t.6.34.6: In that impenetrable darkness the rākṣasas, frenzied with rage, rushed about with tremendous speed, devouring the monkeys.
t.6.34.7: Leaping upon them, those monkeys of terrible fury tore apart with their sharp teeth the horses with golden crests and the banners that resembled tongues of fire.
t.6.34.8: Overcome with rage, they dragged down elephants and elephant-riders and chariots bearing pennants and banners, and tore at them with their teeth.
t.6.34.9: Lakṣmaṇa and Rāma, too, with arrows like venomous serpents, struck down the foremost rākṣasas, both those that could be seen and those that could not.
t.6.34.10: The dust of the earth, shattered by the hooves of horses and stirred up by the rims of chariot wheels, choked the ears and eyes of those who were fighting.
t.6.34.11: As that terrible, hair-raising battle went on, rivers with blood for water and of great swiftness flowed forth there.
t.6.34.12: Then there arose the sound of kettledrums, mṛdaṅgas and paṇavas, mingled with the sound of conches and flutes, a din that seemed truly wondrous.
t.6.34.13: An exceedingly dreadful din arose from the slain and groaning rākṣasas, from the weapons, and from the vānaras.
t.6.34.14: There the battlefield had weapons strewn over it like an offering of flowers; it was hard to make out and hard to set foot upon, a mire of streaming blood.
t.6.34.15: That night became terrible, carrying off monkeys and rākṣasas alike, impossible to get through, like the night of universal destruction for all beings.
t.6.34.16: Then those rākṣasas there, in that dreadful darkness, rushed at Rāma alone, thrilled with excitement, with showers of arrows.
t.6.34.17: The clamor of those enraged warriors, rushing forward and roaring aloud, was a sound like the upheaval of the seven oceans.
t.6.34.18: Of them, Rāma slew six night-rovers with six sharp arrows resembling tongues of fire, in no more than the twinkling of an eye.
t.6.34.20: But those who, struck by Rāma with floods of arrows in all their vital parts, withdrew from the battle there remained with some remnant of life.
t.6.34.19: Yajñaśatru the invincible, Mahāpārśva and Mahodara, the huge-bodied Vajradaṃṣṭra, and those two as well, Śuka and Sāraṇa.
t.6.34.22: But those other heroic Rākṣasas who stood facing Rāma, they too perished on reaching him, like moths that fly into a fire.
t.6.34.21: Then the mighty one, with arrows whose shafts were adorned with gold and which resembled flames of fire, made the directions and the intermediate directions bright.
t.6.34.23: With arrows bearing golden shafts falling in their thousands, the night became brilliantly variegated, like an autumn night lit with fireflies.
t.6.34.24: With the shouts of the rākṣasas and the roars of the monkeys, that night, already dreadful, then became more dreadful still.
t.6.34.25: With that mighty sound swelling on every side, the mountain Trikūṭa, strewn with caves, seemed as if to cry out in reply.
t.6.34.27: But Aṅgada, having come forward in battle to slay the enemy, swiftly struck down Rāvaṇi's charioteer and his horses as well.
t.6.34.26: The huge-bodied Golāṅgūlas, dark as the gloom of night, clasped the night-roaming demons in their arms and went on devouring them.
t.6.34.28: But Indrajit, the great master of illusion, his horses and charioteer slain by Aṅgada, abandoned his chariot and vanished right there.
t.6.34.29: That wicked son of Rāvaṇa, harsh in battle, having gone into invisibility, the heroic son of Rāvaṇa who had received a boon from Brahmā, stupefied with rage, unseen, released sharpened arrows with the splendour of thunderbolts.
t.6.34.30: In the battle, that enraged rākṣasa pierced both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa in all their limbs with terrible arrows made of serpents.
